items.title: Collapsing the set of naturals inside $\mathbb{R}$ to a point gives a quotient of $\mathbb{R}$ that is not locally compact at the collapsed point
The diagonal $x \mapsto (x,x,\dots)$ from $\mathbb{R}$ into $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ is continuous for the product topology and not for the box topology
$x \mapsto x/2$ maps $(0,1]$ into itself, is a $1/2$-contraction, and has no fixed point
Two copies of $\mathbb{R}$ glued along $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ give a non-Hausdorff quotient of a metrizable space, by an open quotient map
Refuted: a pointwise bounded family of continuous functions is equicontinuous. The spikes are bounded by $1$ everywhere and are not equicontinuous at $0$
$\mathbb{Z}$ and $\{n + 1/n : n \ge 2\}$ are disjoint closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ at distance $0$, so the set-to-set distance is not a metric
The open interval $(0,1)$ is totally bounded and not compact, the cover by the intervals $(1/(k+2), 1)$ having no finite subcover
Ascoli–Arzelà for a compact Hausdorff domain
Complete normality, and hence $T_5$, is hereditary
A regular connected covering has deck group $\pi_1(B,b_0)/p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$
The trigonometric loops give $\pi_1(\{(x,y):x^2+y^2=1\},(1,0))\cong\mathbb Z$
Under the ultrafilter lemma and the Axiom of Choice, a metrizable space is Čech-complete exactly when it is completely metrizable
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is not simply connected
Under dependent choice and the ultrafilter lemma, the Stone-Cech compactification maps continuously onto the Samuel compactification
Under dependent choice a normal $T_1$ space is completely regular, so $T_4 \Rightarrow T_{3\frac{1}{2}}$, and together with the implications already proved this is the whole classical chain
The circle as $S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with basepoint $[0]$
Completely regular spaces and Tychonoff ($T_{3\frac{1}{2}}$) spaces
Covering-space actions by disjoint translates of neighbourhoods
Euclidean spheres and closed balls as subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^n$
Hereditary, open-hereditary and closed-hereditary properties of topological spaces
Lifts of maps, paths, and homotopies through a covering map
Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space
Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point
The one-point (Alexandroff) compactification $X^{*} = X \cup \{\infty\}$, whose open sets are the open sets of $X$ together with the complements in $X^{*}$ of the closed compact subsets of $X$
Polygonal schemas and paired boundary edges
Second countability: an at most countable basis for the topology
The standard circle loops $\omega_n(t)=[nt]$ for $n\in\mathbb Z$
Topological group: multiplication and inversion are continuous
Uniform space in the uniform-cover formulation
Urysohn ($T_{2\frac{1}{2}}$) space: distinct points have neighbourhoods with disjoint closures
A surjective circle loop can have degree zero and be nullhomotopic
The bounded real-valued functions on a set, with the supremum metric, form a complete metric space
Every nonempty closed subset $A$ of $\mathbb{R}$ is the zero set of $x \mapsto d(x, A)$ and the intersection of the open sets $\{x : d(x,A) < 1/(n+1)\}$, worked for $[0,1]$ and for $\{0\}$
The discrete, indiscrete, cofinite, cocountable, particular-point and Sierpinski topologies placed in the connectedness hierarchy
Dini's theorem applied to a nondecreasing sequence of piecewise linear approximations on $[0,1]$, and what fails when the limit is not continuous
On a finite compact Hausdorff space a unital separating algebra contains every scalar-valued function
Under the Axiom of Choice, the Hilbert cube is compact, Polish, and universal for separable metrizable spaces
Assuming choice, $\omega_1$ is countably compact, noncompact, and not paracompact
The post-office metric $d(x,y) = \|x\| + \|y\|$ for $x \ne y$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and its isolated points
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the product of $n$ copies of the real line: the product topology is the Euclidean topology and the projections are continuous, open and surjective
Sierpinski space is $T_0$ and normal but neither $T_1$ nor regular: normality without $T_1$ implies nothing
The cocountable topology on $\mathbb{R}$ is $T_1$, has unique sequential limits, and is neither Hausdorff nor regular nor normal
The Hawaiian earring is locally path-connected but has no universal cover

$\mathbb{R}$ with the half-open intervals $[a,b)$ as a basis is not compact and, assuming the Axiom of Countable Choice, is Lindel\"of, while its square is not Lindel\"of, the antidiagonal being an uncountable closed discrete subspace
Endpoint-duplicating functions on $[0,1]$ become all continuous functions on the endpoint quotient
FALSE: every retract is a deformation retract
FALSE: in every metric space the closure of $B(x,r)$ is the closed ball of radius $r$
FALSE: every fundamental group is abelian
FALSE: every topology is induced by some metric
FALSE: the product topology and the box topology agree on every product
FALSE: the closure of a path-connected subspace is path-connected
In a Hausdorff space a sequence converges to at most one point
Based circle loops of equal degree are path-homotopic

A subset of a metric space is open in the subspace metric exactly when it is the trace of an open set of the ambient space, and it is compact as a metric space in its own right exactly when every family of open subsets of the ambient space covering it, indexed or not, has finitely many members covering it
Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, a countable intersection of completely metrizable subspaces is completely metrizable
$|d(x,A) - d(y,A)| \le d(x,y)$, so the distance to a fixed nonempty set is $1$-Lipschitz
Every finite power of an at most countable set is at most countable
Jones's bound: under choice, a closed discrete subspace of a normal space cannot have more subsets than a dense set has subsets
The lower-limit line has a clopen basis, is regular, and is Lindelöf under countable choice
Under choice, Ornstein's second construction turns a point-finite metric open cover into a locally finite open refinement
A space is normal if and only if every closed $A$ inside an open $U$ admits an open $V$ with $A \subseteq V \subseteq \overline{V} \subseteq U$
For a nonempty path-connected locally path-connected semilocally simply connected space, the path-class projection is a covering map
Arbitrary products preserve $T_0$, $T_1$, and Hausdorffness
Regularity is hereditary, without a hidden $T_1$ hypothesis
For continuous maps into a convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$, the straight-line formula defines a continuous homotopy
On an ordinal with its order topology the sets $[0,\beta]$ and $(\alpha,\beta]$ form a basis of clopen sets, the isolated points are exactly the non-limit ordinals, and the space is Hausdorff
Every cluster point of an ultrafilter is a limit of that ultrafilter
Every cluster point of a universal net is a limit of that net
Every compact space is paracompact
The general real function-algebra definition agrees with the published compact-metric definition
A retract induces an injection on fundamental groups, and a deformation retract induces an isomorphism
Completeness belongs to the metric; complete metrizability is characterised on a later page
Conventions on this page, and the one implication of the classical chain that is not available at this point in the reading order
Alexander's subbase lemma: if every cover by members of a fixed subbasis has a finite subcover then the space is compact; the proof is an application of Zorn's lemma
Under choice, a space is metrizable if and only if it is regular, $T_1$, and has a $\sigma$-discrete basis
Classification of compact connected surfaces
Assuming the ultrafilter lemma, an arbitrary product of compact Hausdorff spaces is compact

A continuous image of a compact space is compact; a continuous real-valued map on a nonempty compact space attains a maximum and a minimum; and a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism
Every completely normal space is normal, and every perfectly normal space is normal
The image of a compact metric space under a continuous map is compact, and so is the image of any compact subset
Lifting criterion for maps from path-connected locally path-connected spaces
If $X$ is a locally compact metric space then the evaluation map is continuous for the compact-open topology
$\pi_1(X\times Y,(x_0,y_0))\cong\pi_1(X,x_0)\times\pi_1(Y,y_0)$
Heine-Cantor: a continuous map from a compact metric space to any metric space is uniformly continuous

In a locally compact Hausdorff space every point has a neighbourhood base of compact sets, every open subspace and every closed subspace is locally compact, every open set around a point contains an open set with compact closure inside it, and every compact set sits inside an open set with compact closure
Arbitrary unions and finite intersections of open sets are open, open balls are open and closed balls are closed
There is no retraction of the closed disk onto the unit circle
Existence and uniqueness of path lifts through a covering map
Products commute with subspaces; for infinite nonempty families, the closure identity $\overline{\prod A_i}=\prod \overline{A_i}$ uses the Axiom of Choice
$p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is a covering map with translated interval sheets
Seifert–van Kampen identifies the fundamental group with a group pushout
A space is $T_1$ if and only if every singleton is closed, if and only if every finite subset is closed, if and only if its topology contains the cofinite topology
Any two continuous maps into a nonempty convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are homotopic by straight lines
A union of connected subspaces with a point in common is connected, and so is a union of a family in which every member meets a fixed connected member
